title: Pennsylvania will require labels on AI-generated ads
content:
On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad — whether it’s a still image, video, audio, or text — that “has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence” to include a label in the same format as the ad itself. That applies to TV commercials from multi-billion-dollar companies, as well as restaurants’ ugly, crowded flyers about their wing specials.
Pennsylvania will require labels on AI-generated ads
Pennsylvania’s AI Deceptive Advertising Act leaves a lot of loopholes.
Pennsylvania is one of the first states to require disclosures on AI content. And it requires those labels regardless of where an ad was created. So you might see disclosures pop up in commercials in other states if they’re also expected to air in Pennsylvania.
The law leaves many loopholes, though. For one, what constitutes “significantly modified” is subjective. There is also a carve-out for “parody, satire, commentary or criticism,” as well as anything that is “evidently fictional.” Again, what “evidently fictional” means is unclear. The wording also suggests only content that “uses synthetic content in a manner that creates a false consumer perception” about a product or service would require a disclosure. Again, leaving questions about what qualifies as “false” under the law and who makes those decisions.
The office of State Senator Nick Pisciottano, who introduced the bill, did not immediately return a request for comment.

report.summary: Pennsylvania now requires labels on ads significantly generated or modified by AI, though vague terms and exemptions may limit enforcement.
report.background: Generative AI has made it cheap to produce realistic images, video, audio, and copy for advertising, raising concerns about deceptive marketing and consumer trust. With no comprehensive federal disclosure rule for AI-generated ads, states are beginning to act. Pennsylvania is among the first to mandate labels, signing the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act after it was introduced by State Senator Nick Pisciottano. The law arrives as regulators and industry groups increasingly push provenance standards such as Content Credentials, while platforms and advertisers experiment with synthetic media. Its broad scope—covering text, images, audio, and video—signals that state-level AI transparency rules may proliferate, creating a patchwork that national advertisers must navigate.
key_points: The law covers any ad—still image, video, audio, or text—that has been “significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence.” Disclosures must appear in the same format as the ad, applying to major TV commercials and small-business flyers alike.

Pennsylvania is one of the first states to require AI disclosures in advertising. Because labels are required regardless of where an ad was created, commercials made elsewhere may need disclosures if they are expected to air in Pennsylvania.

Enforcement may be complicated by subjective language. “Significantly modified” is undefined, and the law carves out parody, satire, commentary, criticism, and content that is “evidently fictional,” without clarifying those terms.

The wording suggests disclosures apply only when synthetic content “creates a false consumer perception” about a product or service. That leaves open questions about what counts as false and who decides, making the law’s practical reach uncertain.
report.impact: The law adds a compliance layer for advertisers and AI tool developers, who may need to build labeling, metadata, and review workflows into ad production. National campaigns could face Pennsylvania-specific disclosures even when created elsewhere, encouraging provenance tools and legal review. For developers, demand may grow for content credentials, watermarking, and audit logs that document AI modifications. For regular users, labels could improve transparency, but vague definitions and broad exemptions may produce inconsistent disclosures and a false sense of security. The bigger signal is regulatory fragmentation: states may keep passing AI ad rules while federal guidance remains absent, forcing industry to standardize or navigate many regimes.
report.tools: Watch provenance and labeling tools such as the C2PA Content Credentials standard and its open-source c2patool, Adobe Content Authenticity, Google SynthID for watermarking, and Truepic for verified media capture. Compliance teams should also track state AI advertising bills and FTC guidance, since Pennsylvania’s law may inspire similar disclosure requirements elsewhere.
